research_material:
I make a timetable every Sunday and quit by Tuesday
how do you study when your phone is right there

pain_points: Planning systems fall apart within days (Sunday timetable abandoned by Tuesday)
Lack of accountability or follow-through on productivity systems
Difficulty maintaining routines beyond initial motivation

ideas.idea: Post-Tuesday Reality Check: Why your Sunday plan dies and what actually works instead
ideas.pain_point: Planning systems fall apart within days
ideas.unique_angle: Most productivity content ignores the 48-hour failure point—we'd normalize it and show what contingency plans look like

ideas.idea: The Micro-Timetable: 2-day study schedules instead of weekly (reload every 48 hours)
ideas.pain_point: Planning systems fall apart within days
ideas.unique_angle: Flips the framework entirely—shorter cycles that match actual attention span instead of fighting it

ideas.idea: Phone Physics: Visual breakdown of what actually happens in your brain when your phone is in arm's reach vs. another room
ideas.unique_angle: Explains the science without being preachy, shows distance matters more than willpower

ideas.idea: The Phone Hostage System: Tactical methods college students are already using to lock their phone away during study blocks
ideas.unique_angle: User-generated tactics instead of generic 'delete apps' advice—actual peer solutions

ideas.idea: Accountability Theater vs. Real Accountability: Why telling yourself you'll follow a plan doesn't work, and what external systems do
ideas.pain_point: Lack of accountability or follow-through on productivity systems
ideas.unique_angle: Calls out the illusion of self-discipline without judgment, shows structural vs. motivational fixes

ideas.idea: The 72-Hour Check-in: Simple weekly audit post (did the plan survive? what killed it?) with zero shame framing
ideas.pain_point: Lack of accountability or follow-through on productivity systems
ideas.unique_angle: Makes failure data visible and normal instead of hidden, treats it as debugging not weakness

ideas.idea: Why Your Routine Breaks: Common collapse points mapped to specific days/weeks (week 1 dip, mid-semester burnout triggers)
ideas.pain_point: Difficulty maintaining routines beyond initial motivation
ideas.unique_angle: Predicts failure windows so students can brace for them instead of being blindsided

ideas.idea: The Drift & Reset Protocol: Lightweight framework for restarting when routine inevitably breaks
ideas.pain_point: Difficulty maintaining routines beyond initial motivation
ideas.unique_angle: Assumes failure and designs recovery steps instead of pretending consistency is realistic

ideas.idea: Study Space Hacks: Rearranging dorm/apartment to physically separate you from your phone (no fancy furniture required)
ideas.unique_angle: Environmental design tip—shaping space instead of relying on willpower alone

ideas.idea: The 'Phone Graveyard': Show how different study spaces (library corner vs. dorm desk) change distraction likelihood with student examples
ideas.unique_angle: Real location breakdowns tied to actual distraction risk, not just generic 'go to the library' advice

top_picks.idea: The Micro-Timetable: 2-day study schedules instead of weekly (reload every 48 hours)
top_picks.reason: Directly solves the expressed pain (quitting by Tuesday) by redesigning the system to match actual behavior instead of fighting it. Instantly actionable and reframes 'failure' as a feature.

top_picks.idea: The Phone Hostage System: Tactical methods college students are already using to lock their phone away during study blocks
top_picks.reason: Directly addresses the second question with peer-sourced solutions rather than generic advice. High shareability and relatability for the procrastinator audience.

top_picks.idea: Why Your Routine Breaks: Common collapse points mapped to specific days/weeks
top_picks.reason: Bridges both pain points by validating the experience and providing predictive framework. Positions the brand as understanding the actual struggle, not just selling productivity fantasy.

missing_info: What specifically kills the timetable on Tuesday? (Overwhelm, boredom, unexpected events, unrealistic expectations?)
When studying with phone nearby, what apps/notifications are the biggest pull?
Have any of these students tried phone-blocking apps, physical separation, or other tactics? What worked/failed?
Are there specific study contexts mentioned? (Dorm, library, home, group settings?)
What's the semester timeline—do they struggle equally in week 1 vs. midterms vs. finals?

hooks.text: Your weekly planner is why you're still procrastinating.
What if you only planned 2 days at a time?
48 hours. That's all your brain can actually commit to.
Everyone's using weekly planners. You're about to switch.
Why your Sunday planning session fails by Wednesday (spoiler: scope).
Micro-timetables hit different than your Notes app chaos.
Two days. Reload. Repeat. No 5-day guilt trips.
Students who study this way finish 3 days earlier.
Your brain's procrastination deadline is shorter than you think.
Syllabus says weekly deadlines. Your focus span says 48 hours.

winner.text: 48 hours. That's all your brain can actually commit to.
winner.reasoning: This hook flips the script from a personal failure (procrastination) into a neuroscience fact, making procrastinators feel understood rather than blamed. College students recognize this as permission to work *with* their real attention span instead of fighting it, which is the core appeal of the micro-timetable concept.

runner_up.text: Your weekly planner is why you're still procrastinating.
runner_up.reasoning: Direct pain-point call-out that names the enemy (their existing system) rather than their weakness. Safer because it doesn't require them to accept a cognitive limitation—just swap tools. Still high-intent but slightly less psychologically sticky than the winner.

script.script:
[HOOK - 0-3 sec]
[ON-SCREEN TEXT: 48 HOURS]
Your brain can actually commit to 48 hours. That's it.

[PAUSE]
[CUT]

[PROBLEM - 3-7 sec]
You're planning your entire semester like it's a Netflix series you'll binge. Spoiler: you won't.

[CUT]

[VALUE - 7-20 sec]
Here's what actually works: break everything into 48-hour sprints. Not weekly. Not monthly. Two days.

[PAUSE]

Why? Your brain stops lying to itself after 48 hours. You can't fake momentum. You either did the work or you didn't.

[CUT]

Start with ONE assignment. Pick the 48-hour window. Commit. Done.

[PAUSE]

[CTA - 20-23 sec]
[ON-SCREEN TEXT: FOLLOW FOR THE FULL SYSTEM]
Follow for the complete breakdown of how to actually stick to this.

[CUT]
script.viewer_takeaway: Your procrastination problem isn't motivation—it's planning horizon. Breaking tasks into 48-hour sprints makes deadlines real and removes the ability to self-deceive about progress.

cover_options: Bold red countdown timer showing '48' with a student looking stressed in the background, text overlay: '48 HOURS'
Split-screen: left side shows a chaotic semester calendar, right side shows a clean 48-hour sprint block, text overlay: 'FORGET EVERYTHING ELSE'

frame_plan.visual_direction: Large bold red/white text center-screen. Quick cut to close-up of person's face looking determined. Subtle timer animation in corner counting down from 48:00.
Quick montage: person scrolling semester calendar, Netflix app opening, overwhelmed facial expressions. Fast cuts (0.5-1 sec each). High-energy, slightly chaotic B-roll.
Person at desk writing/planning on paper. Zoom in on notepad showing '48-HOUR WINDOW' written down. Clean, organized aesthetic. Slow, intentional pacing.
Person nodding, pointing at camera. Text appears as they speak. Cut to checkmark appearing on whiteboard/paper. Confident, matter-of-fact energy.
Close-up of hand circling single task on list. Highlighter coming across assignment. Zoom out to show person looking relieved/satisfied.
Person looking directly at camera with slight smile. Follow icon animation appears on-screen. End frame freeze with both text lines visible simultaneously.

assets_needed: B-roll: phone scrolling through calendar app
B-roll: person pointing at camera (confident expression)
Stock footage or custom: timer animation (48:00 countdown)
Stock footage or custom: highlighter on paper
Music: upbeat, millennial-friendly, 120+ BPM track (problem section faster, value section slower)
Sound design: subtle timer ticks, pen scratches, text pop SFX

justifications.clarity: Hook lands instantly with a specific number; the 48-hour concept is concrete and immediately graspable.
justifications.retention: Problem section is relatable but fairly generic ('Netflix series'); value section needs stronger emotional payoff to keep scrollers past second 7.
justifications.save_potential: Core insight (brain stops lying after 48 hours) is novel enough to bookmark; actionable first step elevates it beyond theory.
justifications.shareability: Solves a real problem but lacks the 'wow' factor or humor that makes procrastinators tag friends; feels more educational than laugh-worthy.
justifications.audience_fit: Directly addresses semester planning, Netflix procrastination, and momentum-faking—all core pain points of your target audience.
justifications.cta_strength: Follow request is clear and low-friction, but 'full system' is vague; no hint of what that system contains creates friction in the decision.

weaknesses.issue: Value section lacks proof or result—viewers hear '48-hour sprints work' but see no before/after or concrete outcome.
weaknesses.fix: Add a quick stat or relatable result at 12-15 sec: 'People using 48-hour sprints go from 3 all-nighters a semester to zero' or 'One student went from D's to B's in 3 weeks.' Show result on-screen as text overlay while person nods.

weaknesses.issue: CTA is too vague ('full system')—doesn't tell viewer what they're actually getting or why they should tap follow now instead of later.
weaknesses.fix: Replace 'FOLLOW FOR THE FULL SYSTEM' with 'FOLLOW FOR: The exact 48-hr planner template + 3 ways your brain sabotages deadlines.' Specificity increases urgency.

weaknesses.issue: Problem section ('lying to yourself about Netflix binges') is relatable but undercuts emotional stakes—needs one more layer to justify urgency.
weaknesses.fix: Expand problem at 4-6 sec to: 'You're planning your whole semester like it's a Netflix series you'll binge. Meanwhile, you're already failing two classes by week 3.' Quick text overlay: 'FAILING BY WEEK 3.' Creates tension before solution appears.

captions: Your brain stops lying after 48 hours. You either did the work or you didn't. Here's how to break your semester into sprints that actually stick → [FOLLOW] for the template + the 3 psychology tricks that kill procrastination.

Stop planning your semester like a Netflix binge. 48-hour sprints are how real students go from 3 all-nighters a semester to zero. Follow for the exact system—including the planner template—that works when willpower doesn't.
growth.final_call_reason: Core insight is strong and audience fit is excellent, but the value section needs a concrete proof point (stat, result, or psychological mechanism) and the CTA must move from 'full system' to specific deliverables to maximize follow conversion; these two fixes will lift retention and shareability from 6–7 to 8+.
